title: The Power Transformer: Equivalent Circuit, Efficiency & Voltage Regulation

content.aim: To understand the operational performance of a single-phase step-down power transformer, experimentally determine its equivalent circuit parameters (series resistance, leakage reactance, core-loss shunt resistance, and magnetizing reactance) using non-destructive Open-Circuit and Short-Circuit tests, and evaluate its voltage regulation and electrical energy conversion efficiency under varied loading conditions and power factors.
objectives: Perform the Open-Circuit (No-Load) Test on the low-voltage winding to determine core hysteresis and eddy current losses (\(\mathit{P}_{core}\)), no-load power factor (\(\cos\theta _{0}\)), core resistance (\(\mathit{R}_{c}\)), and magnetizing reactance (\(\mathit{X}_{m}\)).

Perform the Short-Circuit Test on the high-voltage winding to determine full-load copper loss (\(\mathit{P}_{cu,FL}\)), equivalent series resistance (\(\mathit{R}_{eq1}\)), equivalent leakage reactance (\(\mathit{X}_{eq1}\)), and equivalent impedance (\(\mathit{Z}_{eq1}\)).
Synthesize the complete per-phase equivalent circuit referred to both primary and secondary windings with numerical values inserted.
Predict voltage regulation across load currents from 0% to 125% of rated load for unity, lagging (\(0.8 lag\)), and leading (\(0.8 lead\)) power factors.

Predict and plot the efficiency curve (\(\eta\) vs \(\mathit{I}_{2}\)) and experimentally verify the Maximum Efficiency Theorem, proving that peak efficiency occurs when variable copper loss equals constant core loss (\(\mathit{P}_{cu} = \mathit{P}_{core}\)).
Perform a direct on-load resistive test and compare predicted values of regulation and efficiency with actual measured physical meter readings.

theory.text:
Electromagnetic Induction & Turns Ratio

The power transformer is a static electromagnetic energy conversion device based on Faraday's Law of Mutual Induction. When an alternating voltage \(\mathit{v}_{1}(t)\) is applied to the primary winding, it produces an alternating magnetic flux \(Φ(t) = Φ_{m} \sin(\omega t)\) within the closed, high-permeability laminated silicon steel core. This flux links both the primary and secondary windings, inducing counter-electromotive forces:

Induced EMFs & Transformation Ratio
\[\mathit{e}_{1} = -\mathit{N}_{1} \frac{dΦ}{dt} \Rightarrow \mathit{E}_{1} = 4.44 f \mathit{N}_{1} Φ_{m}\]

\[\mathit{e}_{2} = -\mathit{N}_{2} \frac{dΦ}{dt} \Rightarrow \mathit{E}_{2} = 4.44 f \mathit{N}_{2} Φ_{m}\]

\[a = \frac{\mathit{N}_{1}}{\mathit{N}_{2}} = \frac{\mathit{E}_{1}}{\mathit{E}_{2}} \approx \frac{\mathit{V}_{1}}{\mathit{V}_{2}} = \frac{\mathit{I}_{2}}{\mathit{I}_{1}} = \frac{220 V}{110 V} = 2.0\]
Exact Equivalent Circuit Referred to Primary

A practical physical transformer deviates from an ideal transformer due to finite winding resistance, magnetic leakage flux, core hysteresis, and eddy currents (Fig 1):

• Primary Series Branch (\(\mathit{r}_{1}, \mathit{x}_{1}\)): Resistance of primary copper wire (\(\mathit{r}_{1}\)) and leakage reactance (\(\mathit{x}_{1}\)) caused by magnetic flux lines that link only the primary winding without penetrating the core.
• Shunt Excitation Branch (\(\mathit{R}_{c}, \mathit{X}_{m}\)): Connected across the induced EMF to model core losses and magnetizing current:

\(\mathit{R}_{c}\) (Core Loss Resistance): Accounts for energy dissipated as heat due to alternating magnetic hysteresis (\(\mathit{P}_{h} ∝ f \mathit{B}_{m}^{1.6}\)) and circulating eddy currents (\(\mathit{P}_{e} ∝ f^{2} \mathit{B}_{m}^{2} t^{2}\)).
\(\mathit{X}_{m}\) (Magnetizing Reactance): Accounts for the reactive volt-amperes required to establish the alternating mutual magnetic flux \(Φ_{m}\) in the ferromagnetic core.
• \(\mathit{R}_{c}\) (Core Loss Resistance): Accounts for energy dissipated as heat due to alternating magnetic hysteresis (\(\mathit{P}_{h} ∝ f \mathit{B}_{m}^{1.6}\)) and circulating eddy currents (\(\mathit{P}_{e} ∝ f^{2} \mathit{B}_{m}^{2} t^{2}\)).
• \(\mathit{X}_{m}\) (Magnetizing Reactance): Accounts for the reactive volt-amperes required to establish the alternating mutual magnetic flux \(Φ_{m}\) in the ferromagnetic core.
• Referred Secondary Series Branch (\(\mathit{r}_{2}', \mathit{x}_{2}'\)): Secondary resistance and leakage reactance referred to the primary by multiplying by the square of the turns ratio (\(a^{2}\)):

Impedance Referral Rules
\(\mathit{r}_{2}' = a^{2} \mathit{r}_{2} = (2.0)^{2} \mathit{r}_{2} = 4 \mathit{r}_{2}\)

\(\mathit{x}_{2}' = a^{2} \mathit{x}_{2} = (2.0)^{2} \mathit{x}_{2} = 4 \mathit{x}_{2}\)

\(\mathit{R}_{eq1} = \mathit{r}_{1} + \mathit{r}_{2}' = \mathit{r}_{1} + a^{2} \mathit{r}_{2}\)

\(\mathit{X}_{eq1} = \mathit{x}_{1} + \mathit{x}_{2}' = \mathit{x}_{1} + a^{2} \mathit{x}_{2}\)
Non-Destructive Parameter Extraction: Open-Circuit & Short-Circuit Tests

Determining the four equivalent circuit parameters does not require loading the transformer to its full \(1.2 kVA\) rating; they are extracted with high precision using two specialized non-destructive tests:

1. Open-Circuit (No-Load) Test (O.C. Test):

The test is conducted by applying rated voltage to the Low-Voltage (LV, \(110V\)) winding while keeping the High-Voltage (HV) winding on open circuit. Because the HV side is open, no secondary current flows (\(\mathit{I}_{2} = 0\)). The input current \(\mathit{I}_{oc}\) is merely the tiny no-load exciting current (\(3–5\%\) of rated). The copper loss caused by \(\mathit{I}_{oc}\) in the primary winding (\(\mathit{I}_{oc}^{2} \mathit{r}_{LV}\)) is negligible (\(< 0.1 W\)). Consequently, the wattmeter reading \(\mathit{P}_{oc}\) represents strictly the constant core (iron) loss of the transformer (\(\mathit{P}_{oc} \approx \mathit{P}_{core}\)):

Open-Circuit Formulations
\[\cos\theta _{0} = (\mathit{P}_{oc}) / (\mathit{V}_{oc} \mathit{I}_{oc})\]

\[Reactive Magnetizing Power: \mathit{Q}_{0} = √((\mathit{V}_{oc} \mathit{I}_{oc})^{2} - \mathit{P}_{oc}^{2})\]

\[\mathit{R}_{c(LV)} = \frac{\mathit{V}_{oc}^{2}}{\mathit{P}_{oc}} = (\mathit{V}_{oc}) / (\mathit{I}_{oc} \cos\theta _{0})\]

\[\mathit{X}_{m(LV)} = \frac{\mathit{V}_{oc}^{2}}{\mathit{Q}_{0}} = (\mathit{V}_{oc}) / (\mathit{I}_{oc} \sin\theta _{0})\]

To refer these shunt parameters to the High-Voltage (primary, \(220V\)) side:

\[\mathit{R}_{c1} = a^{2} \cdot \mathit{R}_{c(LV)} = 4 \cdot \mathit{R}_{c(LV)} and \mathit{X}_{m1} = a^{2} \cdot \mathit{X}_{m(LV)} = 4 \cdot \mathit{X}_{m(LV)}\]

2. Short-Circuit Test (S.C. Test):

The Low-Voltage (LV) winding is short-circuited using a thick copper jumper cable. A very low AC voltage (\(\mathit{V}_{sc}\), typically \(5–10\%\) of rated) is cautiously applied to the High-Voltage (HV) winding and increased until the ammeter indicates rated full-load primary current (\(\mathit{I}_{sc} = \mathit{I}_{1,FL} = 5.45 A\)). Because the applied voltage \(\mathit{V}_{sc}\) is tiny, the mutual core flux \(Φ_{m} ∝ \mathit{V}_{sc}\) is less than 7% of normal, rendering core hysteresis and eddy losses completely negligible (\(< 1\%\)). Therefore, the wattmeter reading \(\mathit{P}_{sc}\) represents strictly the full-load copper loss dissipated in the primary and secondary winding resistances:

Short-Circuit Formulations
\[\mathit{Z}_{eq1} = \frac{\mathit{V}_{sc}}{\mathit{I}_{sc}}\]

\[\mathit{R}_{eq1} = \mathit{r}_{1} + \mathit{r}_{2}' = \frac{\mathit{P}_{sc}}{\mathit{I}_{sc}^{2}}\]

\[\mathit{X}_{eq1} = \mathit{x}_{1} + \mathit{x}_{2}' = √(\mathit{Z}_{eq1}^{2} - \mathit{R}_{eq1}^{2})\]
Performance Characteristics: Voltage Regulation & Efficiency

1. Voltage Regulation (\(VR\)): Defined as the arithmetic difference between the secondary terminal voltage at no-load (\(\mathit{V}_{2,NL}\)) and full-load (\(\mathit{V}_{2,FL}\)), expressed as a percentage of full-load voltage:

Voltage Regulation Formulations
\[\%VR = (\mathit{V}_{2,NL} - \mathit{V}_{2,FL}) / (\mathit{V}_{2,FL}) \times 100\%\]

\[Approximate Formula: \%VR \approx (\mathit{I}_{2} (\mathit{R}_{eq2} \cos\theta _{2} ± \mathit{X}_{eq2} \sin\theta _{2})) / (\mathit{V}_{2}) \times 100\%\]

where the plus sign (\(+\)) applies to lagging power factors (inductive loads causing terminal voltage to drop), and the minus sign (\(-\)) applies to leading power factors (capacitive loads, which can cause secondary voltage to rise above no-load voltage—a negative regulation).

2. Efficiency (\(\eta\)): The ratio of real electrical power delivered to the load to the total real power absorbed from the mains:

Transformer Efficiency Formulation
\[\eta = \frac{\mathit{P}_{out}}{\mathit{P}_{in}} \times 100\% = (\mathit{V}_{2} \mathit{I}_{2} \cos\theta _{2}) / (\mathit{V}_{2} \mathit{I}_{2} \cos\theta _{2} + \mathit{P}_{core} + \mathit{I}_{2}^{2} \mathit{R}_{eq2}) \times 100\%\]
Mathematical Proof of Maximum Efficiency Condition

To prove the theoretical condition that maximizes transformer efficiency, express efficiency as a function of secondary load current \(\mathit{I}_{2}\) at a constant terminal voltage \(\mathit{V}_{2}\) and constant load power factor \(\cos\theta _{2}\):

\[\eta = \frac{\mathit{V}_{2} \mathit{I}_{2} \cos\theta _{2}}{\mathit{V}_{2} \mathit{I}_{2} \cos\theta _{2} + \mathit{P}_{core} + \mathit{I}_{2}^{2} \mathit{R}_{eq2}} = \frac{1}{1 + (\mathit{P}_{core}) / (\mathit{V}_{2} \mathit{I}_{2} \cos\theta _{2}) + (\mathit{I}_{2} \mathit{R}_{eq2}) / (\mathit{V}_{2} \cos\theta _{2})}\]

Efficiency \(\eta\) reaches its maximum when the denominator \(D(\mathit{I}_{2})\) is minimized:

\[D(\mathit{I}_{2}) = 1 + \frac{\mathit{P}_{core}}{\mathit{V}_{2} \mathit{I}_{2} \cos\theta _{2}} + \frac{\mathit{I}_{2} \mathit{R}_{eq2}}{\mathit{V}_{2} \cos\theta _{2}}\]

Differentiating \(D(\mathit{I}_{2})\) with respect to \(\mathit{I}_{2}\) and setting the derivative equal to zero:

\[\frac{d D(\mathit{I}_{2})}{d \mathit{I}_{2}} = 0 - \frac{\mathit{P}_{core}}{\mathit{V}_{2} \mathit{I}_{2}^{2} \cos\theta _{2}} + \frac{\mathit{R}_{eq2}}{\mathit{V}_{2} \cos\theta _{2}} = 0\]

Multiplying through by \(\mathit{V}_{2} \cos\theta _{2}\):

\[\frac{\mathit{P}_{core}}{\mathit{I}_{2}^{2}} = \mathit{R}_{eq2} \Rightarrow \mathit{I}_{2}^{2} \mathit{R}_{eq2} = \mathit{P}_{core}\]

Maximum Efficiency Theorem
\[\mathit{P}_{cu} = \mathit{P}_{core}\]

\[Maximum efficiency occurs when the variable copper loss equals the constant core (iron) loss.\]

The load current at which peak efficiency occurs is given by:

Load Current for Peak Efficiency
\[\mathit{I}_{2(max \eta )} = \mathit{I}_{2,FL} \times √(\frac{\mathit{P}_{core}}{\mathit{P}_{cu,FL}})\]

procedure: Safety & Terminal Identification: Identify the High-Voltage (\(220V\)) and Low-Voltage (\(110V\)) terminal pairs of the single-phase transformer. Ensure the HV terminals are insulated, safely shrouded, and left completely open.

O.C. Circuit Metering: Connect the LV (\(110V\)) winding to the Variac output through a low-range ammeter (\(0–1.0A\)), a low-power-factor wattmeter (\(150V, 1.0A\)), and voltmeter (\(0–150V\)). Ensure the Variac is set to zero volts.
Execution: Switch ON the mains supply. Gradually increase the Variac voltage until the voltmeter reads rated LV voltage of exactly \(110.0 V\).

Data Recording: Record open-circuit voltage \(\mathit{V}_{oc}\), no-load current \(\mathit{I}_{oc}\), and no-load core loss power \(\mathit{P}_{oc}\) into Table 308.1. Reduce the Variac to zero volts and switch OFF the supply.
Secondary Shorting: Firmly bolt a thick copper shorting strap across the Low-Voltage (\(110V\)) secondary terminals. Ensure the connection has near-zero contact resistance.

S.C. Circuit Metering: Connect the High-Voltage (\(220V\)) primary winding to the Variac output in series with a high-current ammeter (\(0–10A\)), a standard wattmeter (\(250V, 10A\)), and a low-range AC voltmeter (\(0–30V\)).

Cautious Energization: Ensure the Variac dial is set to absolute zero. Switch ON the supply. Very slowly and cautiously rotate the Variac knob while keeping your eyes fixed on the ammeter. Stop advancing the instant line current reaches rated full-load value (\(\mathit{I}_{sc} = 5.45 A\)).

Data Recording: Immediately log short-circuit voltage \(\mathit{V}_{sc}\), current \(\mathit{I}_{sc}\), and power \(\mathit{P}_{sc}\) into Table 308.2. Instantly reduce the Variac to zero and switch OFF the supply.

Load Bank Connection: Connect the HV primary winding to the fixed \(220.0V\) AC mains. Connect the secondary LV winding to the stepped secondary load resistor bank through an ammeter, voltmeter, and load wattmeter.

Load Sweep: Starting from no-load (\(\mathit{I}_{2} = 0\)), incrementally switch on load resistor steps to draw \(2.73A, 5.45A, 8.18A\), and \(10.91A\) (full load). At each step, record terminal voltage \(\mathit{V}_{2}\), load current \(\mathit{I}_{2}\), and secondary power. Compute direct experimental regulation and efficiency, and compare with Table 308.4 predictions.
precautions: Lethal Step-Up Voltage on Open-Circuit Test: When \(110V\) is applied to the LV winding during the O.C. test, the open HV terminals generate a full, lethal \(220V\) potential across the open lugs. Never touch open HV terminals while the transformer is energized! Insulate terminals with safety shrouds.

Short-Circuit Over-Current Surge Danger: During the S.C. test, the impedance between primary terminals is merely \(2.66 \Omega\). Accidental application of full \(220V\) will unleash a catastrophic short-circuit current of \(220 / 2.66 = 82.7 Amperes\)—more than 15 times rated current—instantly vaporizing the winding and tripping substation breakers. Always confirm zero Variac position before power-up.

Low Power Factor Wattmeter Necessity: In the O.C. test, \(\cos\theta _{0} \approx 0.37\). Standard wattmeters designed for unity power factor will yield severe scale compression and calibration errors. A dedicated Low Power Factor (LPF) wattmeter must be used.
content.discussion:
The experimental results obtained from testing the \(1.2 kVA, 220V/110V\) power transformer provide rigorous verification of classical electromagnetic transformer modeling.

From the Open-Circuit Test (Table 308.1), the constant core loss was established as \(\mathit{P}_{core} = 18.50 W\). Because magnetic core flux is constant as long as primary voltage is fixed, this \(18.50 W\) hysteresis and eddy current loss remains perfectly constant regardless of whether the transformer is uncoupled or delivering maximum full-load current.

From the Short-Circuit Test (Table 308.2), full-load copper loss was measured as \(\mathit{P}_{cu,FL} = 42.80 W\). Unlike core loss, copper loss is entirely variable, scaling strictly with the square of the load current: \(\mathit{P}_{cu}(\mathit{I}_{2}) = (\frac{\mathit{I}_{2}}{\mathit{I}_{2,FL}})^{2} \times 42.80 W\).

Verification of the Maximum Efficiency Condition

According to our theoretical derivation in Section 4.5, maximum conversion efficiency must occur at the specific load fraction where variable copper loss equals constant core loss (\(\mathit{P}_{cu} = \mathit{P}_{core} = 18.50 W\)):

\[\mathit{x}_{opt} = √(\frac{\mathit{P}_{core}}{\mathit{P}_{cu,FL}}) = √(\frac{18.50}{42.80}) = \sqrt{0.4322} = 0.6574 (65.74\% of Full Load)\]

The corresponding secondary load current for maximum efficiency is:

\[\mathit{I}_{2(max \eta )} = 0.6574 \times 10.91 A = 7.17 A\]

Examining Table 308.4 and Graph 308.1 proves this theorem with remarkable precision: efficiency climbs from \(93.41\%\) at 25% load, reaches an absolute peak plateau of \(95.52\%\) at \(7.17 A\), and then gently tapers to \(95.14\%\) at full load as \(I^{2} R\) copper loss begins to outpace core loss. Industrial distribution transformers are intentionally engineered with this loss ratio (\(\mathit{P}_{core} \approx 0.4–0.5 \mathit{P}_{cu,FL}\)) so that peak efficiency aligns with the typical \(60–75\%\) average daily loading cycle.

Voltage Regulation & Power Factor Dependency

The voltage regulation characteristics reveal the decisive influence of load power factor:

• At Unity Power Factor (\(\cos\theta _{2} = 1.0\)): Voltage regulation is strictly positive and moderate (\(VR = +3.57\%\)), caused solely by the internal ohmic resistance drop across \(\mathit{R}_{eq2} = 0.360 \Omega\). Full-load terminal voltage drops to \(106.1 V\).
• At Lagging Power Factor (\(\cos\theta _{2} = 0.8 lag\)): Inductive load current produces an in-phase voltage drop across leakage reactance \(\mathit{X}_{eq2} = 0.560 \Omega\), compounding the resistance drop. Voltage regulation worsens significantly to \(+6.20\%\), dropping secondary terminal voltage to \(103.2 V\).
• At Leading Power Factor (\(\cos\theta _{2} = 0.8 lead\)): The leading capacitive current creates a voltage drop across leakage reactance that is \(180^\circ\) out of phase with the resistive drop:

\[\Delta V = \mathit{I}_{2}(\mathit{R}_{eq2} \cos\theta _{2} - \mathit{X}_{eq2} \sin\theta _{2}) = 10.91(0.360 \times 0.8 - 0.560 \times 0.6) = 10.91(0.288 - 0.336) = -0.52 V\]

Regulation becomes negative (\(-0.48\%\)), meaning secondary terminal voltage actually rises above no-load voltage (rising to \(110.52 V\)), an empirical confirmation of the Ferranti effect in inductive/capacitive coupled circuits.
content.conclusion: Experiment 308 successfully characterized the performance, efficiency, and regulation of a \(1.2 kVA, 220V / 110V\) single-phase power transformer. The equivalent circuit parameters were experimentally extracted: series parameters \(\mathit{R}_{eq1} = 1.441 \Omega , \mathit{X}_{eq1} = 2.238 \Omega\), and shunt parameters \(\mathit{R}_{c1} = 2616.2 \Omega , \mathit{X}_{m1} = 1054.2 \Omega\). Full-load efficiency reached an impressive \(95.14\%\) at unity power factor, with peak efficiency of \(95.52\%\) occurring precisely at \(65.74\%\) of rated load where variable copper loss equaled constant core loss (\(18.50 W\)), mathematically and empirically proving the Maximum Efficiency Theorem. Voltage regulation was shown to be heavily power-factor dependent, shifting from \(+6.20\%\) under \(0.8\) lagging load to \(-0.48\%\) voltage rise under \(0.8\) leading load. Excellent correspondence (\(< 1.5\%\) deviation) was established between predicted equivalent circuit models and direct physical loading measurements.

questions.question: Draw the complete equivalent circuit of the transformer inserting all numerical parameter values referred to the primary side.
questions.answer:
Complete Synthesized Numerical Equivalent Circuit (Referred to Primary HV Side, 220V):

Numerical Parameters (Primary Referred)
Primary Series Resistance: \(\mathit{r}_{1} = \mathit{R}_{eq1} / 2 = 1.441 / 2 = 0.720 \Omega\)

Referred Secondary Resistance: \(\mathit{r}_{2}' = a^{2} \mathit{r}_{2} = \mathit{R}_{eq1} / 2 = 0.720 \Omega\)

Primary Leakage Reactance: \(\mathit{x}_{1} = \mathit{X}_{eq1} / 2 = 2.238 / 2 = 1.119 \Omega\)

Referred Secondary Leakage Reactance: \(\mathit{x}_{2}' = a^{2} \mathit{x}_{2} = \mathit{X}_{eq1} / 2 = 1.119 \Omega\)

Core Loss Shunt Resistance: \(\mathit{R}_{c1} = a^{2} \mathit{R}_{c(LV)} = 4 \times 654.1 = 2616.2 \Omega\)

Magnetizing Shunt Reactance: \(\mathit{X}_{m1} = a^{2} \mathit{X}_{m(LV)} = 4 \times 263.6 = 1054.2 \Omega\)

Ideal Turns Ratio: \(a = 220 V : 110 V = 2 : 1\)

questions.question: Theoretical Question: Show mathematically using differential calculus that transformer efficiency is maximum at a load which makes copper losses equal to constant (core) losses.
questions.answer:
Rigorous Mathematical Proof:

Let transformer output power be \(\mathit{P}_{out} = \mathit{V}_{2} \mathit{I}_{2} \cos\theta _{2}\), constant core loss be \(\mathit{P}_{i} = \mathit{P}_{core}\), and total copper loss be \(\mathit{P}_{cu} = \mathit{I}_{2}^{2} \mathit{R}_{eq2}\).

The efficiency equation is:

\[\eta = \frac{\mathit{V}_{2} \mathit{I}_{2} \cos\theta _{2}}{\mathit{V}_{2} \mathit{I}_{2} \cos\theta _{2} + \mathit{P}_{i} + \mathit{I}_{2}^{2} \mathit{R}_{eq2}}\]

Dividing numerator and denominator by \(\mathit{I}_{2}\):

\[\eta = \frac{\mathit{V}_{2} \cos\theta _{2}}{\mathit{V}_{2} \cos\theta _{2} + \frac{\mathit{P}_{i}}{\mathit{I}_{2}} + \mathit{I}_{2} \mathit{R}_{eq2}}\]

For constant terminal voltage \(\mathit{V}_{2}\) and power factor \(\cos\theta _{2}\), efficiency \(\eta\) is maximized when the denominator \(y(\mathit{I}_{2})\) is minimized:

\[y(\mathit{I}_{2}) = \mathit{V}_{2} \cos\theta _{2} + \frac{\mathit{P}_{i}}{\mathit{I}_{2}} + \mathit{I}_{2} \mathit{R}_{eq2}\]

Differentiating \(y(\mathit{I}_{2})\) with respect to load current \(\mathit{I}_{2}\) and equating to zero:

\[\frac{dy}{d \mathit{I}_{2}} = 0 - \frac{\mathit{P}_{i}}{\mathit{I}_{2}^{2}} + \mathit{R}_{eq2} = 0\]

\[\mathit{R}_{eq2} = \frac{\mathit{P}_{i}}{\mathit{I}_{2}^{2}} \Rightarrow \mathit{I}_{2}^{2} \mathit{R}_{eq2} = \mathit{P}_{i}\]

\[\mathit{P}_{cu} = \mathit{P}_{core}\]

To confirm that this represents a true minimum for the denominator (and hence maximum efficiency), evaluate the second derivative:

\[\frac{d^{2} y}{d \mathit{I}_{2}^{2}} = +\frac{2 \mathit{P}_{i}}{\mathit{I}_{2}^{3}} > 0 (Since \mathit{P}_{i} > 0 and \mathit{I}_{2} > 0)\]

Because the second derivative is strictly positive, the denominator is minimized, rigorously proving that transformer efficiency is strictly maximized when variable copper loss equals constant core loss.

questions.question: Compute and compare the predicted values of voltage regulation and efficiency with the direct physical meter readings obtained during the on-load test at full rated load (\(\mathit{I}_{2} = 10.91 A\), unity PF).
questions.answer:
Predicted vs Direct Measurement Comparison:

• Predicted from Equivalent Circuit (Table 308.4):

\[\mathit{V}_{2,FL(pred)} = 110.0 - \mathit{I}_{2} \mathit{R}_{eq2} = 110.0 - (10.91 \times 0.360) = 110.0 - 3.93 = 106.07 V\]

\[\%VR_{pred} = \frac{110.0 - 106.07}{110.0} \times 100\% = 3.57\%\]

\[\eta _{pred} = \frac{1200}{1200 + 18.50 + 42.80} \times 100\% = \frac{1200}{1261.3} \times 100\% = 95.14\%\]
• Direct Meter Readings from On-Load Test:
Measured Full-Load Voltage: \(\mathit{V}_{2,meas} = 105.80 V\).

Measured Primary Input Power: \(\mathit{P}_{in,meas} = 1215.0 W\).

Measured Secondary Output Power: \(\mathit{P}_{out,meas} = 105.80 V \times 10.91 A = 1154.3 W\).

\[\%VR_{meas} = \frac{110.0 - 105.80}{110.0} \times 100\% = 3.82\%\]

\[\eta _{meas} = \frac{1154.3}{1215.0} \times 100\% = 95.00\%\]

Discrepancy Evaluation: The predicted voltage regulation deviates by only \(0.25\%\), and the efficiency deviates by only 0.14%. This extraordinary agreement validates the predictive accuracy of the per-phase equivalent circuit model.

questions.question: Explain "All-Day Efficiency" (Operational Energy Efficiency) of a distribution transformer and why it differs profoundly from commercial power efficiency.
questions.answer:
Commercial power efficiency is calculated at a single instantaneous loading instant (\(\eta = \mathit{P}_{out} / \mathit{P}_{in}\)). However, electrical distribution transformers (pole-mounted or pad-mounted utility units) remain permanently energized 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, but experience widely fluctuating consumer loads:

• During off-peak hours (midnight to 6 AM), load is near zero, but the core loss (\(\mathit{P}_{core}\)) is continuously consumed 24 hours a day!
• During peak evening hours, heavy load causes substantial copper loss (\(I^{2} R\)), but only for 4 to 6 hours.

Therefore, distribution transformers are judged by All-Day Efficiency (\(\eta _{all-day}\)), which is the ratio of total energy delivered in kilowatt-hours (kWh) over a 24-hour cycle to the total energy absorbed:

All-Day Energy Efficiency
\(\eta _{all-day} = (Energy Output in 24 Hours (kWh)) / (Energy Output in 24 Hours (kWh) + (\mathit{P}_{core} \times 24 h) + ∑ (\mathit{I}_{2}^{2} \mathit{R}_{eq2} \times \mathit{t}_{i})) \times 100\%\)

Because the core loss operates continuously for 24 hours while copper loss operates only intermittently, distribution transformer designers deliberately minimize core losses by utilizing expensive high-permeability amorphous metal or cold-rolled grain-oriented (CRGO) silicon steel cores, accepting slightly higher copper resistance. This shifts the peak efficiency point to approximately \(50\%\) of rated load, maximizing the 24-hour all-day energy efficiency.

learnings: Separation of Core and Copper Losses: Complete understanding of how O.C. and S.C. tests isolate magnetic hysteresis/eddy losses from electric winding ohmic losses without requiring full-load mechanical dissipation.
Loss Optimization Mechanics: The calculus-based principle of designing transformers for specific peak efficiency loading points (commercial distribution vs base-load generator step-up).
Power Factor Impact on Terminal Voltage: Practical observation of why inductive loads drag voltage down while capacitive loads cause voltage swell (Ferranti-like rise).
Laboratory Safety Discipline: Understanding dangerous step-up voltage potentials during low-voltage excitation of multi-winding electrical equipment.
